title: Texas Teen Ananya Nagendra Builds Ant-Based Food Waste Digester With 83% Efficiency
excerpt: The 18-year-old Indian-American student from Plano tested four ant species and designed a prototype aerobic digester that could reduce methane emissions from landfills at a fraction of the cost of conventional systems.
body:
• Ananya Gulur Nagendra, 18, from Plano, Texas, designed an ant-based aerobic digester that achieved 83% efficiency in food waste processing
  • She tested four ant species and found Camponotus castaneus consumed the most waste due to its high metabolic rate
  • Food waste generates about 58% of methane emissions from landfills, making alternative processing methods critical
  • Nagendra was named a 2026 Regeneron Science Talent Search finalist, selected from 2,612 entrants nationwide

Ananya Gulur Nagendra, an 18-year-old student from Plano, Texas, developed a prototype ant-based aerobic digester for landfill food waste that tested at approximately 83% efficiency. The project, which earned her a place among the finalists of the 2026 Regeneron Science Talent Search, asks a disarmingly simple question: can one of nature's smallest scavengers help solve one of its largest waste problems?

The Problem With Landfill Food Waste

Food waste accounts for about 58% of methane emissions from landfills, according to the Society for Science. When organic material is buried under anaerobic conditions, it decomposes into methane — a greenhouse gas roughly 80 times more potent than carbon dioxide over a 20-year horizon. The scale of the problem is enormous: the United States alone sends approximately 60 million tons of food waste to landfills annually.

https://x.com/AsianetNewsSN/status/2089397302771569108

Rather than pursue a mechanical or chemical solution, Nagendra looked to biology. Ants are natural scavengers that actively seek out and consume organic food materials. Her research examined whether their feeding behaviour could be harnessed in a controlled system to divert food waste from the decomposition pathway that produces methane.

Four Species, One Winner

Nagendra began by testing four different ant species to measure how much food waste each could break down per ant per day. The experiments identified Camponotus castaneus — a species of carpenter ant — as the strongest candidate. It consumed the greatest amount of food waste among the tested species and had the highest metabolic rate, making it the most efficient biological processor for the system she was designing.

The comparative testing was central to the project's scientific rigor. Nagendra did not assume ants would work as waste processors. She gathered measurable evidence showing which species performed best, then used those findings to build a mathematical model estimating potential methane reduction.

From Model to Prototype

Using C. castaneus data, Nagendra designed and built a prototype aerobic digester — a system that allows decomposition in the presence of oxygen, with ants serving as the primary biological agents rather than conventional mechanical or chemical methods. Tests of the prototype found it was about 83% efficient at processing the food waste it received.

Nagendra also estimated that a scaled-up version of the system could cost less than $50,000 — a fraction of the price of conventional composting or anaerobic digestion facilities, which can run into millions of dollars for municipal-scale operations.

A Regeneron Science Talent Search Finalist

The 2026 Regeneron Science Talent Search drew 2,612 entrants. From that pool, 300 were named scholars. The finalist group — which included Nagendra — was selected from 35 schools across 15 states, with more than $1.8 million in prizes available, including a top prize of $250,000. Finalists were chosen based on the originality and creativity of their research, as well as their achievements and leadership, according to the Society for Science.

"Her research could point toward a new approach to reducing the environmental impact of food waste in landfills."

— Society for Science

What's Next

The prototype is an early-stage demonstration rather than a commercially deployable system. Further research would need to examine performance with different types and quantities of food waste, ant colony behaviour over extended periods, and how the approach scales. But for an 18-year-old who started with a question about ants and ended with a working prototype, the journey from species testing to mathematical modelling to a functional digester represents a substantial contribution to an emerging field of bio-inspired waste management.
